title: TrafficClaw: Generalizable Urban Traffic Control via Unified Physical Environment Modeling

paper.title: TrafficClaw: Generalizable Urban Traffic Control via Unified Physical Environment Modeling
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Urban traffic control is a system-level coordination problem spanning heterogeneous subsystems, including traffic signals, freeways, public transit, and taxi services. Existing optimization-based, reinforcement learning (RL), and emerging LLM-based approaches are largely designed for isolated tasks, limiting both cross-task generalization and the ability to capture coupled physical dynamics across subsystems.
We argue that effective system-level control requires a unified physical environment in which subsystems share infrastructure, mobility demand, and spatiotemporal constraints, allowing local interventions to propagate through the network. To this end, we propose TrafficClaw , a framework for general urban traffic control built upon a unified runtime environment. TrafficClaw integrates heterogeneous subsystems into a shared dynamical system, enabling explicit modeling of cross-subsystem interactions and closed-loop agent–environment feedback. Within this environment, we develop an LLM agent with executable spatiotemporal reasoning and reusable procedural memory, supporting unified diagnostics across subsystems and continual strategy refinement. Furthermore, we introduce a multi-stage training pipeline with supervised initialization and agentic RL with system-level optimization, further enabling coordinated and system-aware performance. Experiments demonstrate that TrafficClaw achieves robust, transferable, and system-aware performance across unseen traffic scenarios, dynamics, and task configurations. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/TrafficClaw .

Introduction Traffic control is a fundamental component of intelligent transportation systems, governing the allocation of mobility resources across space and time to balance efficiency, safety, equity, and sustainability ( Wei et al., 2019 ; Siri et al., 2021 ) . Applications such as traffic signal control, freeway management, and public transit scheduling directly affect congestion, energy consumption, emissions, and service reliability, while also shaping long-term travel behavior and urban structure. As cities evolve toward multi-mode and demand-responsive mobility ecosystems, traffic control has transitioned from isolated optimization tasks to a system-level decision-making problem over tightly coupled subsystems ( e.g., traffic signals, freeways, public transit, and taxi services). Existing approaches can be broadly categorized into optimization-based methods, reinforcement learning (RL), and LLM-based agents. Classical methods rely on analytical models and hand-crafted formulations, while RL approaches learn adaptive policies via trial-and-error but require substantial task-specific reward engineering and exhibit limited transferability ( Farazi et al., 2021 ; Wang and Sun, 2022 ; Jin et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2017 ; Belletti et al., 2017 ) . Recent LLM-based agents introduce language-driven reasoning and flexible tool use, improving interpretability and adaptability ( Lai et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . However, most methods remain fundamentally task-isolated, requiring significant redesign of environments, workflows, and training pipelines across subsystems, thereby limiting cross-task generalization and preventing system-level optimization. These limitations motivate a shift from task-specific controllers to autonomous agents capable of reasoning, interacting, and adapting across tasks. Recent LLM-agent research suggests that such generalization can emerge from diverse task exposure ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Xi et al., 2025 ) , long-horizon tool-augmented reasoning ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Pang et al., 2025 ) , and learning from rich interaction dynamics ( Froger et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) . Building on these advances, we argue for a general traffic intelligence agent that operates within a unified environment, where cross-subsystem interactions generate system-level feedback to guide learning and decision-making. However, existing LLM agents predominantly operate in separate digital environments ( e.g., search engines ( Li et al., 2025a ) or Minecraft ( Dong et al., 2024 ) ), where tasks are modular and largely independent. In contrast, urban traffic systems are physically grounded and tightly coupled: local interventions inevitably induce system-level feedback across subsystems. Simply increasing task diversity across isolated environments therefore fails to capture such structured interdependencies and cannot support unified diagnostics or coordinated system-level control. Bringing general-purpose agents into traffic control therefore raises three fundamental challenges. First, generalizable traffic control requires a unified environment. Unlike loosely coupled digital environments, urban mobility emerges from the interaction of multiple traffic subsystems and mobility demand fluctuations that share physical infrastructure and spatiotemporal constraints. Consequently, generalizable traffic control requires an interactive environment that jointly integrates heterogeneous subsystems into a unified environment, where control actions induce long-horizon, network-wide feedbacks. Such an environment is essential for exposing agents to cross-subsystem dependencies and enabling coordinated control strategies to emerge through iterative interactions. Second, even within a unified environment, the agent must reason consistently across heterogeneous subsystem dynamics and objectives. Different subsystems exhibit distinct spatial structures and temporal behaviors ( e.g., intersections involve localized turning conflicts and queue spillback, whereas public transit systems evolve through station-level passenger accumulation and schedule-dependent dynamics). This heterogeneity renders isolated, task-specific representations insufficient for capturing how congestion, demand, and control interventions propagate across the network. Consequently, generalizable traffic control requires a unified modeling framework that supports coherent diagnosis of cross-subsystem traffic and enables coordinated decision-making within a shared analytical interface, thereby optimizing system-level efficiency. The third challenge concerns unified training under heterogeneous and potentially conflicting objectives. Different traffic subsystems are associated with distinct optimization goals and feedback signals, making it non-trivial to jointly optimize them within a single learning framework. Firstly, improvements in one subsystem may systematically degrade performance in others, thereby leading to sub-optimal system-level outcomes ( e.g., aggressive bus scheduling toward demand hotspots may improve service but undermines traffic signal efficiency on the roads). Secondly, task-specific rewards are often designed independently, leading to biased optimization towards short-horizon or easily optimized objectives. Effective system-level traffic control therefore requires learning protocols that explicitly account for system-level improvement, prompting cross-objective trade-offs while preserving individual performance. To this end, we propose TrafficClaw , an OpenClaw-like ( Steinberger and Contributors, 2025 ) runtime agent for general urban traffic control built upon a unified urban traffic environment. TrafficClaw is embedded in an integrated platform that consolidates heterogeneous traffic subsystems under shared physical infrastructure, spatiotemporal constraints, and multi-mode mobility demand. This design allows interventions in one subsystem to propagate across others, creating network-wide feedback loops that reflect the coupled dynamics of urban traffic. By situating the agent in this closed-loop environment, TrafficClaw performs iterative cycles of perception, analytical reasoning, action execution, and feedback-driven optimization, enabling system-level traffic control grounded in real-time spatiotemporal conditions. Building on this environment, we design a unified traffic control agent with two tightly coupled components: executable spatiotemporal reasoning and spatiotemporal memory. Rather than relying on fixed feature encoders tailored to individual subsystems, the agent performs a unified data-driven analysis across spatial, temporal, and cross-subsystem dimensions via executable code. This analytical process yields structured diagnostics that explicitly capture how congestion, demand, and control interventions propagate across subsystems, enabling coherent reasoning under heterogeneous dynamics. These diagnostics further support a feedback-driven decision loop, in which candidate actions are iteratively evaluated and refined through environment feedback prior to deployment. In parallel, the agent maintains a spatiotemporal memory that distills recurring patterns, coordination strategies, and failure modes into reusable procedural knowledge and episodic context caches. Through the integration of unified feedback-driven reasoning and experience accumulation loops, the agent self-improves optimization strategies and system-level traffic efficiency iteratively. To translate analytical reasoning into actionable policies under real-world traffic dynamics, we adopt a multi-stage training strategy. We first generate diverse multi-task trajectories across spatial regions, temporal patterns, and task configurations, providing supervised signals that bootstrap generalizable reasoning over heterogeneous subsystems. The agent is then optimized via agentic RL within the unified environment, guided by a system-level reward that integrates traffic efficiency and coordination quality, enabling uniformed optimization across heterogeneous subsystems with potentially conflicting objectives. This interaction-driven process aligns decision-making with system-level goals while improving robustness under dynamic conditions. As a result, the learned policies are both transferable and system-aware. (1) We introduce a unified urban traffic environment that integrates heterogeneous subsystems into a shared physical system, explicitly modeling how local interventions propagate through cross-subsystem coupling. To our knowledge, this is the first framework that enables generalizable traffic control with LLM agents in a unified environment.
